what_its_for: Sotalol is used to treat certain irregular heartbeat problems (called arrhythmias). It helps your heart beat more regularly and at a steadier rate. It belongs to a group of medicines called beta-blockers and also works to stabilize the heart's electrical signals.
how_to_take: Take sotalol exactly as your doctor prescribed. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. It is very important to take this medicine at evenly spaced times — for example, every 12 hours if you take it twice a day. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablets unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is okay. If you are using the liquid form (Sotylize), carefully measure your dose using the measuring device that came with the medicine.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the dose that is right for you based on your heart condition and kidney function. A common starting dose for adults is 80 mg twice a day, but your doctor may slowly increase this over time. Your first doses may be given in a hospital so your heart can be monitored closely. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if your next scheduled dose is more than 8 hours away. If your next dose is less than 8 hours away, skip the missed dose and take the next one at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. Missing doses or stopping this medicine suddenly can be dangerous for your heart.
storage: Store sotalol tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid form (Sotylize) at room temperature and use it within 3 months of opening. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Do not stop taking sotalol suddenly without talking to your doctor first — stopping abruptly can cause serious heart problems. Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and affect your heart rhythm. Do not take antacids containing aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox or Mylanta) within 2 hours of taking sotalol, as they can make the medicine less effective. Avoid taking other heart rhythm medicines, certain antibiotics (like azithromycin), antidepressants, or antipsychotic medicines unless your doctor specifically approves them, as combining these can cause a dangerous heart rhythm. Be careful driving or using machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause dizziness.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a very fast, slow, or pounding heartbeat; fainting or feeling like you might faint; severe dizziness or lightheadedness; shortness of breath that is new or getting worse; chest pain or tightness; swelling of your feet or ankles; sudden unexplained weight gain; signs of low blood sugar if you are diabetic (since sotalol can mask these symptoms); or any new or unusual symptoms. Tell your doctor immediately if you feel your heart rhythm has changed or feels worse.
when_it_works: Sotalol begins working within a few hours of your first dose, but it may take several days to weeks before your heart rhythm is fully under control. Because starting this medicine can be tricky and needs careful monitoring, many people begin it in a hospital setting. You may not feel any different as the medicine works — that is normal. Do not stop taking it just because you feel well. It is controlling your heart rhythm even when you have no symptoms.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Sotalol is removed from your body by your kidneys. If your kidneys do not work well, your doctor will adjust your dose or how often you take it. Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and falls, so extra caution is needed. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Sotalol can pass into breast milk and may affect your baby. Your doctor will help weigh the risks and benefits. Children: Dosing in children is based on body size and must be carefully calculated by a doctor. Diabetes: Sotalol can hide some warning signs of low blood sugar (like a fast heartbeat), so monitor your blood sugar closely and tell your doctor you are diabetic.
